from manim import *

class TeachingScene(Scene):
    def setup_layout(self, title_text, lecture_lines):
        # BASE
        self.camera.background_color = "#000000"
        self.title = Text(title_text, font_size=28, color=WHITE).to_edge(UP)

        self.lecture.to_edge(LEFT, buff=0.2)
        self.add(self.lecture)

        # Define fine-grained animation grid (4x4 grid on right side)

        center_y = (tl_pos[1] + br_pos[1]) / 2

class Section3Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        self.setup_layout("The Hilbert Curve: Optimization", [
            "The Hilbert curve follows a U-shape.",
            "It preserves locality between adjacent points.",
            "This makes it efficient for spatial indexing."
        ])
        
        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        # Display a basic Hilbert curve iteration #FFFFFF.
        def get_hilbert_path(order=1):
            path = []
            def recursive_hilbert(x, y, xi, xj, yi, yj, n):
                if n <= 0:
                    path.append(np.array([x + (xi + yi)/2, y + (xj + yj)/2, 0]))
                else:
                    recursive_hilbert(x, y, yi/2, yj/2, xi/2, xj/2, n-1)
                    recursive_hilbert(x+xi/2, y+xj/2, xi/2, xj/2, yi/2, yj/2, n-1)
                    recursive_hilbert(x+xi/2+yi/2, y+xj/2+yj/2, xi/2, xj/2, yi/2, yj/2, n-1)
                    recursive_hilbert(x+xi/2+yi-1, y+xj/2+yj-1, -yi/2, -yj/2, -xi/2, -xj/2, n-1)
            recursive_hilbert(0, 0, 1, 0, 0, 1, order)
            return VMobject().set_points_as_corners(path)

        hilbert = get_hilbert_path(order=2)
        hilbert.set_color("#FFFFFF")
        self.place_in_area(hilbert, "B2", "E5", scale_factor=1.5)
        self.play(Create(hilbert), self.lecture[0].animate.set_color("#FFFFFF"))

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        # Highlight the recursion step clearly #FF00FF.
        # Simple animation to show the "U" shape recursive nature
        self.play(hilbert.animate.set_color("#FF00FF"), self.lecture[1].animate.set_color("#FF00FF"))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        # Show local locality preservation #00FFFF.
        dots = VGroup(*[Dot(color="#00FFFF", radius=0.05) for _ in range(2)])
        # Position dots near each other on the curve
        dots[0].move_to(hilbert.get_points()[0])
        dots[1].move_to(hilbert.get_points()[1])
        self.add(dots)
        self.play(self.lecture[2].animate.set_color("#00FFFF"))
        self.play(FadeIn(dots))
        self.play(dots.animate.shift(RIGHT*0.2))
        self.wait(1)

sections.title: The Dimensional Paradox (0:00-0:45)
sections.content: Introduce the intuition-defying concept: Can a 1D line fill a 2D square? Establish prerequisite: the concept of 'continuity' and 'dimension'. Explain that traditionally, lines have no area, but space-filling curves challenge this by visiting every point in a region.
sections.example: Visualize a thin thread being infinitely folded into a square until the empty space disappears.

sections.title: The Peano Curve Construction (0:45-2:00)
sections.content: Explain the iterative process: starting with a simple segment and applying a recursive rule. Show how a single line segment is divided into 9 sub-segments, which are then reconnected. Emphasize that as iterations approach infinity, the 'path' covers the entire area.
sections.example: An animated 'snake' character that grows by subdividing its own body into smaller copies to cover a checkerboard grid.

sections.title: The Hilbert Curve: Optimization (2:00-3:30)
sections.content: Introduce the Hilbert curve as a more 'local' version of the space-filling concept. Explain the recursive logic (U-shape transformation). Crucially, explain how this curve preserves locality—points close on the 1D line are usually close in the 2D space.
sections.example: A robotic vacuum cleaner following a Hilbert path to ensure it visits every floor tile efficiently without backtracking.

sections.title: Real-World Applications (3:30-4:30)
sections.content: Discuss practical utility: Mapping multidimensional data to 1D arrays (Database indexing, Cache optimization). Explain why this is better than 'row-major' order for spatial queries.
sections.example: A database system using a space-filling curve to store GPS coordinates, allowing 'nearby' locations to be retrieved with a single memory read.

sections.title: Summary & Philosophical Takeaway (4:30-5:00)
sections.content: Reiterate: Space-filling curves are limit objects. They demonstrate how continuous paths can be 'dense' in a space. End with the concept of fractal dimension—where a curve starts looking like a surface.
sections.example: A final visual showing a 1D line morphing into a solid square, summarizing the transition from sequence to area.
